title: Atypical chest pain treated as unstable angina

source.citation: Munasinghe BM, Fernando UPM, Kumar T, Huruggamuwa C, Kuruppu KARL, Hewawasam GGC. An unusual case of a traumatic splenic rupture masquerading as myocardial ischemia: a case report. Int J Emerg Med. 2022;15(1):63.

presentation.chiefComplaint: Atypical chest pain and left shoulder pain for 3 days
presentation.hpi: Previously healthy woman with 3 days of atypical chest pain and pain in the left shoulder. She reports no sweating or other autonomic symptoms, no breathlessness and no cough or fever. Asked directly, she denies any trauma.
pmh: No significant medical history (ASA physical status 1; BMI 23 kg/m²)

exam: 18 h after admission (on aspirin, clopidogrel and enoxaparin): sudden collapse, BP 70/40 mm Hg, pulse 120/min and of very low volume

imaging.finding: Splenic laceration with an expanding subcapsular haematoma and haemoperitoneum

ecg: T-wave inversion in II, III and aVF; no dynamic change on repeat; normalised within 24 h of surgery

diagnosis.primary: AAST grade IV splenic laceration with haemoperitoneum after a low fall onto the left upper abdomen, presenting late as chest and left shoulder pain mimicking unstable angina

management: Treated as unstable angina: aspirin 300 mg, clopidogrel 300 mg and atorvastatin 40 mg loading, enoxaparin 60 mg SC twice daily; admitted to the medical unit
Sublingual glyceryl trinitrate on the ward for persistent pain
At collapse: oxygen and massive transfusion protocol
On haematology advice: IV tranexamic acid 10 mg/kg and protamine sulfate 1 mg/kg
Emergency laparotomy: two capsule-to-hilum lacerations with a large haematoma (AAST grade IV), about 3.5 L blood loss; splenectomy
Massive transfusion: 6 units red cells, 600 mL plasma, 20 units cryoprecipitate and an adult pool of platelets
ICU; extubated after 10 h; back to the ward on postoperative day 2
Pneumococcal, meningococcal and Haemophilus influenzae type b vaccination at the 2-week follow-up
outcome: Uncomplicated recovery; ECG normalised within 24 h and coronary angiography was normal; no sepsis or surgical complications at 1-year follow-up.
teachingPoints: Left shoulder pain with chest or upper abdominal pain can be referred diaphragmatic irritation from blood (Kehr sign): think spleen.
Trivial falls can cause major splenic injury that declares itself days later; ask explicitly and repeatedly about trauma, since patients may not mention it.
Hypovolaemia and anaemia can cause ischaemic-looking ECG changes; atypical pain with a negative troponin should widen the differential before antithrombotics.
Antiplatelets and anticoagulants given for presumed ACS can turn a contained splenic injury into exsanguination; reverse what you can (protamine for enoxaparin, platelets for clopidogrel).
Haemodynamic instability with haemoperitoneum means operative management; after splenectomy, vaccinate against encapsulated bacteria.

questions.q: What is the most likely cause of her collapse?
questions.extra: 18 h after admission, on aspirin, clopidogrel and enoxaparin: BP 70/40 mm Hg, HR 120/min, severely pale; Hb 3.8 g/dL (13.6 on admission). On re-questioning, she recalls a fall of about 2 feet onto her left upper abdomen when the pain began.
options: Upper GI haemorrhage provoked by dual antiplatelet therapy
Rectus sheath haematoma from enoxaparin injections
Cardiogenic shock from an evolving inferior infarction
Delayed splenic rupture with haemoperitoneum after the fall
questions.explanation: Left shoulder pain (Kehr sign) that began with a fall onto the left upper abdomen, then haemorrhagic shock with haemoglobin falling from 13.6 to 3.8 g/dL, points to a splenic injury bleeding into the peritoneum, accelerated by antithrombotics. A GI or rectus sheath bleed does not explain the pain's onset with the fall, and cardiogenic shock would not cause profound anaemia.

questions.extra: Massive transfusion has started; she remains hypotensive.
options: Contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis
Urgent upper endoscopy to exclude a bleeding ulcer
Coronary angiography for presumed inferior infarction
questions.explanation: In a hypotensive patient, bedside ultrasound finds haemoperitoneum in minutes without interrupting resuscitation; here it showed a splenic laceration with an expanding subcapsular haematoma. CT is for patients stable enough to leave the resuscitation room (ATLS 10th edition).

questions.extra: Ultrasound: splenic laceration with an expanding subcapsular haematoma and haemoperitoneum. She needs ongoing massive transfusion.
options: Non-operative management with serial haemoglobin checks
CT angiography followed by splenic artery embolisation
Repeat ultrasound in 6 hours to assess expansion
questions.explanation: Haemodynamic instability with haemoperitoneum calls for operative management (WSES 2017 splenic trauma guidelines; ATLS 10th edition); non-operative management and angioembolisation are options only for haemodynamically stable patients. At laparotomy she had an AAST grade IV injury with about 3.5 L of blood loss.

questions.q: After splenectomy, which measure most reduces her long-term risk?
options: Lifelong low-dose aspirin for post-splenectomy thrombocytosis
Vaccination against pneumococcus, meningococcus and Haemophilus influenzae b
Annual abdominal ultrasound to look for splenosis
A long-term proton-pump inhibitor after massive transfusion
questions.explanation: Asplenia carries a lifelong risk of overwhelming infection with encapsulated bacteria. After an emergency splenectomy the vaccines are usually given about 2 weeks after surgery, as here, together with advice to seek antibiotics promptly for fever.

evidence.quote: A 39-year-old American Society of Anaesthesiology stage 1
body mass index 23 kg m⁻², South Asian female presented to the ED
with atypical chest pain and left shoulder pain that had lasted for 3 days
in a previously healthy South Asian woman in her late 30s
She did not disclose any autonomic features, difficulty breathing, or cough with fever.
She denied any history of trauma.
On examination, she was not pale.
noninvasive blood pressure, 112/67 mmHg; pulse rate, 88 per minute; peripheral oxygen saturation, 98% on room air; and respiratory rate, 16 per minute
There was no localized tenderness over the chest.
The COVID-19 rapid antigen test result was negative.
The ECG showed ‘T’ inversions in inferior leads (lead II, III, and aVF).
The troponin I titre was negative.
Chest X-ray was normal.
She was diagnosed as having unstable angina considering her persistent symptoms. Loading doses of 300 mg oral aspirin, 300 mg clopidogrel, and 40 mg atorvastatin were prescribed
along with 60 mg subcutaneous enoxaparin twice a day. Subsequently, the patient was transferred to the medical unit.
The repeated ECG did not reveal any dynamic changes.
she complained of persistent symptoms for which sublingual glyceryl trinitrate was administered
Eighteen hours after admission, a sudden haemodynamic collapse was witnessed. Her blood pressure dropped to 70/40 mmHg, and her pulse rate increased to 120 beats per minute
with a very low volume. She was found to be severely pale.
Immediate resuscitation was commenced with supplemental oxygen. A massive transfusion protocol with transfusion of blood and blood products was initiated.
an accidental fall onto a hard surface from an approximate height of 2 feet with impact on her left upper abdomen
An ultrasound scan of the abdomen revealed a splenic laceration with an expanding subscapular haematoma and haemoperitoneum.
Following a haematology consultation, 10 mg/kg tranexamic acid and 1 mg/kg protamine sulfate were intravenously administered.

two linear lacerations extending from the capsule to the hilum were detected in the middle part of the spleen with a large haematoma
An urgent splenectomy was warranted with an ongoing massive blood transfusion.
requiring 6 units of packed red cells, 600 mL of fresh frozen plasma, 20 units of cryoprecipitate, and an adult pool of platelets
Ten hours later, with stable haemodynamics and normalized arterial blood gas analysis, the trachea was extubated.
On postoperative day two, she was transferred back to the ward.
Her ECG changes reverted back to normal within 24 h.
The 2D echocardiogram did not reveal regional wall motion abnormalities.
A coronary angiogram was arranged on an outpatient basis after 2 weeks, which revealed a normal coronary vasculature.
pneumococcal, meningococcal, and Haemophilus influenza b vaccinations arranged at the 2-week follow-up
At the 1-year follow-up, she had been devoid of any life-threatening sepsis or any other surgery-related complications.
a late diagnosis of an advanced grade splenic injury following a trivial trauma initially presented in disguise as acute myocardial ischaemia
